headline: The hostages fly home after 444 days
text: Under the Algiers Accords signed on 19 January, with Algeria as go-between, Iran released the 52 remaining American hostages on 20 January, minutes after Ronald Reagan was sworn in. In return, Iranian gold and securities frozen in the United States are being released through the Algerian central bank, and a tribunal in The Hague will settle claims between the two countries. The hostages were held for 444 days.
imageCaption: Former President Jimmy Carter welcomes the freed American hostages at Wiesbaden, West Germany, January 1981

headline: Apple lays off staff over the troubled Apple III; Jobs becomes chairman
text: The Apple III, the office computer launched in November at 4,340 dollars and more, has been plagued by faults: machines overheat and fail. President Mike Scott laid off employees in February to cut costs, a move co-founder Steve Jobs opposed. Mike Markkula takes over as president and Jobs becomes chairman. The shares, 22 dollars at the December float, have been falling since January.
imageCaption: The Apple III, introduced in 1980

headline: Saturday night TV: 'Wetten, dass..?' starts
text: On 14 February the German channel ZDF broadcast the first 'Wetten, dass..?' (Want to bet?), a Saturday-evening show made together with Austria's ORF and Swiss television. Ordinary people bet that they can do something odd or remarkable, and celebrity guests guess whether they will manage. The host and inventor is Frank Elstner.
imageCaption: The studio of 'Wetten, dass..?' during a show in Graz, November 2014

headline: Buffett: book value up to 400.80 dollars, a third of GEICO
text: In his letter dated 27 February Buffett reports book value per share of 400.80 dollars at the end of 1980, a compound gain of 20.5% a year since present management took over sixteen years ago. Berkshire's insurers now own 7.2 million shares of the car insurer GEICO. The textile business lost money in 1980.
imageCaption: A GEICO claims adjuster inspects a damaged car, 1976

headline: The Rubik's Cube craze
text: In March a speedcubing championship organised by the Guinness Book of Records was held in Munich, and the Rubik's Cube was on the cover of Scientific American. The Hungarian puzzle, invented by Ernő Rubik, went on sale in West Germany in June 1980 and won a special prize of the German Spiel des Jahres award. Shops cannot get enough of it, and books explaining how to solve it are selling well; most people manage only one or two sides.
imageCaption: A Rubik's Cube

headline: BMW, the maker of sporty cars, is now available to you
text: BMW of Munich builds sporty saloons, the 3, 5 and 7 Series, and motorcycles. It sold 339,232 cars in 1980. The Quandt family saved the company from bankruptcy in 1959 and is still its largest shareholder; Eberhard von Kuenheim has run it since 1970. BMW is much smaller than Daimler-Benz but has grown quickly.
imageCaption: A BMW 323i (E21), the sporty 3 Series of 1981

headline: Daimler-Benz, the maker of Mercedes, is now available to you
text: Daimler-Benz of Stuttgart builds Mercedes-Benz cars and is one of the world's biggest makers of trucks and buses. Its new S-Class saloon went into production in December 1979. The Deutsche Bank, Kuwait and the Mercedes-Automobil-Holding are its big shareholders. Gerhard Prinz has been chairman of the board of management since January 1980.

headline: Sandoz profit up 17%, but the Basel parent stagnates
text: On 30 April Sandoz reported 1980 sales up 10.3% to 4.9 billion francs and group profit up 16.8% to 202 million, which management called satisfactory. Dyes weakened in the second half as the economy cooled, while pharmaceuticals and seeds grew faster. The annual report welcomes the end of the franc's overvaluation, which had hurt Swiss exporters; the Basel parent company itself is stagnating.
source: Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 2 May 1981, p. 21 ('«Befriedigendes» Sandoz-Konzern-Ergebnis'), scan data/manual/scans/nzz/NZZ_1981-05-02.pdf (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Marc Moret, head of Sandoz, 1983

headline: Japan is now the world's biggest car maker
text: Japan built more cars than the United States last year, for the first time. Its exports of passenger cars rose from 100,000 in 1965 to 1.8 million in 1975 and have kept climbing, as American drivers hit by two oil shocks turned to small Toyotas, Datsuns and Hondas that use less petrol and break down less. Detroit is losing money and laying off workers, and under pressure from Washington Japan has agreed to limit its car exports to the United States to 1.68 million a year from this month. Cars are only the most visible part: Japanese cameras, television sets and steel are winning markets everywhere.
imageCaption: Toyota Corolla, 2012

headline: WHO adopts a code on baby milk; the Nestlé boycott goes on
text: The World Health Assembly adopted an International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes by 118 votes to 1, with the United States voting against. Activist groups have boycotted Nestlé since July 1977, starting in Minneapolis, accusing it of pushing milk powder on mothers in poor countries where clean water is scarce.
imageCaption: Nestlé's Lactogen baby milk promoted to mothers at a health centre in Africa, around 1975

headline: Apple shares drop 21% from their May high
text: Apple shares fell 21% in June, giving back the rise of April and May, in a flat market. Investors have little to go on beyond the Apple III's reliability problems and talk that IBM, the giant of the computer industry, is preparing its own personal computer. Apple is still growing fast on the Apple II, but the stock market is no longer sure what a young computer company should be worth.

headline: Swiss voters write equal rights for women into the constitution
text: On 14 June Swiss voters approved an article in the federal constitution establishing equal rights for men and women. Swiss women have had the vote at the federal level only since 1971.
imageCaption: Demonstration for women's voting rights in Zurich, February 1966
imageCredit: Hans Gerber, Comet Photo AG / ETH-Bibliothek

headline: Charles and Diana marry before a world audience
text: Prince Charles, heir to the British throne, married Lady Diana Spencer at St Paul's Cathedral in London on 29 July. Two million people lined the route, and the ceremony was watched on television by an estimated 750 million people around the world.
imageCaption: Wedding of Prince Charles and Lady Diana Spencer, 1981

headline: The Fed holds its rate at 19 percent and gold slides below 410
text: The Federal Reserve has held its interest rate near 19 percent since May, as high as it has ever been. Consumer prices in June were 9.6 percent higher than a year earlier, so lenders now earn far more than inflation takes away, and saving pays better than owning gold. Gold averaged 409 dollars in July, 11 percent below June and the lowest since November 1979. The numbers: the Fed's rate 19.0 percent. Inflation 9.7 percent. Unemployment 7.5 percent.
imageCaption: The Fed's interest rate (blue), inflation (red) and unemployment (grey) in the United States, 1955 to July 1981
imageCredit: Chart: Month by Month. Data: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED)

headline: IBM launches the Personal Computer
text: On 12 August IBM presented its Personal Computer, built in about a year by a small team in Boca Raton, Florida. Prices start at 1,565 dollars for a machine with 16 KB of memory. Unusually for IBM, the key parts come from outside: the processor is the 8088 chip of Intel, a Californian chip maker, and the operating system, PC DOS, comes from Microsoft, a small software firm near Seattle that most people have never heard of. Dealers report more orders than they can fill.
imageCaption: "Keeping up with modern times": IBM's advertisement for its Personal Computer with the Charlie Chaplin tramp, 1982
imageCredit: IBM advertisement, from Personal Computing, May 1982 (scan: nosher.net)

headline: Sony shows a camera without film
text: On 25 August Sony unveiled a prototype of the Mavica, an electronic still camera that records pictures as analog video signals instead of on film. Sony has not said when it might go on sale.
imageCaption: A Sony Mavica electronic still camera

headline: The Fed's rate eases to 16 percent, but lending for ten years costs more than ever
text: The Fed's interest rate fell to just under 16 percent in September, from 19 percent in the summer. But investors who lend their money for ten years still demand more than ever before: the yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds averaged 15.3 percent, against about 11.5 percent a year ago, and a 30-year mortgage costs about 18.4 percent. The S&P 500 lost 5 percent in the month as the economy weakens. Shares of companies whose profits lie far in the future, or that depend on borrowing, fell hardest: Apple Computer lost 24 percent, Sony 15, Schlumberger 14 and Intel 13, while steady earners such as McDonald's and Coca-Cola rose. The numbers: the Fed's rate 15.9 percent. Inflation 10.8 percent. Unemployment 7.4 percent.

headline: The 767 flies as airlines suffer
text: The Boeing 767 made its first flight on 26 September. When it was rolled out in August, Boeing had 173 firm orders from 17 customers. It is designed to burn 20 to 30% less fuel than older jets and to need only two pilots, which a presidential task force accepted as safe in July.
imageCaption: The Boeing 767 prototype, September 1981

headline: Doctors' association sells its tobacco shares
text: The American Medical Association sold about 1.4 million dollars of shares in R.J. Reynolds and Philip Morris from its pension fund. Medical students and young doctors had called it contradictory for a medical group to profit from cigarette makers; a spokeswoman said the publicity had hurt.
imageCaption: The American Medical Association's headquarters in Chicago, 2007

headline: Helmut Maucher becomes chief executive
text: Helmut Maucher, a German who ran Nestlé's business in Germany and came to Vevey as general director in 1980, became chief executive of Nestlé in November. He takes over a group under fire for how it sells baby milk.
imageCaption: Helmut Maucher at the St. Gallen Management Symposium, 1985

headline: 1981 in review: high interest rates push shares down 10 percent
text: The S&P 500 fell 10% in 1981 to 122.55, and the Dow closed the year at 875.00, down 9.2%. The Dow had reached 1,024 in April on hopes for Reagan's tax cuts, but the Federal Reserve kept credit tight: its discount rate hit a record 14 percent in May, and the economy slid into recession in the second half. The Fed began to cut the discount rate in November, to 12 percent.
imageCaption: American shares (S&P 500) at the end of each month of 1981: down 9 percent in the year
imageCredit: Chart: Month by Month. Data: Yahoo Finance (^GSPC, month-end closes)

headline: Martial law in Poland
text: General Wojciech Jaruzelski, Poland's Communist Party leader and defence minister, declared martial law on 13 December. Thousands of activists of Solidarity, the free trade union born in the Gdansk shipyard strikes of August 1980, were locked up without trial, among them its leader Lech Walesa; telephone lines were cut, borders and airports closed, and a curfew runs from 7 in the evening to 6 in the morning. On 16 December security forces killed 9 striking miners at the Wujek coal mine. On 23 December the United States imposed economic sanctions on the Polish government.
imageCaption: Martial law in Poland, 1981

headline: Apple replaces the first 14,000 Apple IIIs with a redesigned model
text: Apple is replacing the first 14,000 Apple III computers it sold with a redesigned version that fixes the overheating and faulty circuit boards of the original. The machine, launched a year ago as Apple's step into the office, has sold poorly against the Apple II that still carries the company.
imageCaption: An Apple III with its monitor and external disk drive
imageCredit: Brad from Fort Worth, United States
